episode_title: Tokugawa Yoshimune: The Shogun Who Ate Simple Meals to Save a Near-Bankrupt Shogunate
youtube_title: The Shogun Who Ate Simple Meals to Save a Near-Bankrupt Shogunate
youtube_description:
Japan's most powerful ruler was said to wear plain cotton and eat simple meals, while his government slid into deficit. In 1722, Tokugawa Yoshimune took an extraordinary step: he asked the lords of Japan for their rice. This is the story of the eighth shogun and the Kyoho Reforms, and of how far thrift, a complaint box and a new tax system could carry a government that was running out of money.

Your reporter: Tokio Kamiya, a former newspaper correspondent whose grandfather's brass pocket watch carries him to a single day in Japan's past. He can watch and speak, but he can never change what happens.

scenes.narration: I'm Tokio Kamiya, a former newspaper correspondent. My grandfather, a Kyoto clockmaker, left me a brass pocket watch, and it carries me to any moment in Japan's past, one day at a time. I can watch and speak, but I can never change a thing. For this report, the watch drops me first on Nihonbashi bridge in Edo, 1700. Edo holds perhaps a million people. Porters and samurai crowd the bridge, and boats loaded with rice bales fill the canals. Everything here rests on rice, from samurai pay to farm taxes. Yet the merchants around me trade in gold and silver.

scenes.narration: My watch gives me one day per trip, and none of them falls in 1707. So I rely on the records, and I picture what they describe: Mount Fuji erupts, grey ash drifts down on Edo, and townspeople cover their faces. Relief costs money. The fifth shogun's long reign of costly temples and ceremonies has already strained the treasury, and officials have reduced the gold in the coinage, which pushes prices up. By the 1710s, the shogunate runs deficits, and its leading adviser, the scholar Arai Hakuseki, struggles to repair the damage. Then, in 1716, a death changes everything.

scenes.narration: On another day, I stand on the rampart of Wakayama Castle, in 1705. A young man looks out over the roofs of the town and the sea beyond, two retainers kneeling behind him. This is Tokugawa Yoshimune, born in 1684, fourth son of the lord of Kii, one of the three branch families of the Tokugawa. He was never meant to rule. But a series of deaths in the family has just made him lord of Kii, at twenty. His domain is in financial trouble, and tradition says he will restore it through strict thrift.

scenes.narration: I watch from the far side of the moat as the sun rises over Edo Castle, 1716. The child shogun Ietsugu has died without an heir, and the senior Tokugawa line has ended with him. The family has turned to its branch houses and chosen Yoshimune of Kii, now in his early thirties. I see him climb the stone steps through the great gate, a man who intends to govern himself. Across the courtyard, two older officials in dark formal dress walk away, heads lowered. Manabe Akifusa and Arai Hakuseki will soon leave office, and the old regime goes with them.

scenes.narration: I follow Yoshimune down a long wooden corridor inside Edo Castle. He walks briskly, in plain undyed cotton, eyes straight ahead. Ahead of us, attendants carry bright silk robes and gilded lacquer boxes away to a storeroom. Strict economy has begun, and it starts at the top. Tradition says he keeps his own meals to a simple soup and a few dishes. Whether every detail is true, the message is deliberate: the shogun will not waste what the state does not have. But thrift alone cannot close the gap. The real problem is how the shogunate earns and spends.

I don't know his name, but in 1717 Yoshimune appointed Ooka Tadasuke to this office, responsible for policing and justice in the city. Yoshimune wants capable men, not just well-born ones. In 1723, he introduces the system of tashidaka: an official of modest stipend may hold a high post, and the government makes up the difference only while he serves. Talent can rise without permanently raising anyone's pay.

The treasury cannot even pay its own retainers' stipends. So he does something extraordinary. The man they obey will ask them for their rice. It admits weakness and risks resentment, so he must offer something in return.

scenes.narration: Dawn at the gate, and I stand at the roadside as the edict of 1722 takes effect. Each daimyo must give the shogunate one hundred koku of rice for every ten thousand koku of his domain. Straw bales stream toward the storehouses, while a daimyo procession pours out of the city, eager to go home. That is the price. Sankin-kotai, the alternate attendance in Edo, is cut to six months instead of a full year. Above the gate, Yoshimune watches in silence. The treasury gains rice, the lords save, and the shogunate gives up some control. It lasts until 1730.

scenes.narration: I cannot take you to 1732; the watch has spent my days elsewhere. So I turn to the records. They tell of swarms of insects devastating rice crops across western Japan, and the Kyoho famine begins. I picture pale, eaten stalks and thin farmers crouching with handfuls of ruin. Hunger spreads. The following year, townspeople in Edo smash the premises of a rice dealer they blame for hoarding. The rice economy shows how fragile it is. Yoshimune orders relief and a search for hardy crops. One is rarely grown in the east: the sweet potato.

scenes.narration: Morning at Dojima, Osaka. I push through a canal-side crowd of merchants shouting and bargaining, rice bales stacked high. At the edge stand a few anxious samurai in faded hakama, and their faces explain the problem. The price of rice, in which most samurai are paid, keeps falling relative to other goods, so the warrior class grows poorer while merchants grow richer. In 1730, Yoshimune gives official approval to this very exchange, hoping to steady the market. It earns him the nickname the Rice Shogun. But I think a state cannot order a market to obey.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. So what actually saved the shogunate? I don't think it was the cotton clothes alone. Thrift gave the government credibility, a sign that the shogun would share the sacrifice he demanded. The real gains came from steadier taxes, new fields, the lords' rice and capable officials. In other words, the symbolism opened the door, and the institutions walked through. I think that is a lesson modern Japan knows well. A leader who preaches sacrifice and lives in comfort is ignored. A leader who lives plainly can ask for more than anyone expected.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. The Kyoho Reforms also show the limits of repairing a system without changing it. Yoshimune's tools were old ones: more rice, more tax, tighter spending and firmer control of the countryside. They bought time. Peasant protests became more frequent in the decades that followed, the warrior class stayed in debt to merchants, and the economy kept moving toward money. Later, Tanuma Okitsugu would try the opposite and embrace commerce. I think patching a system is not the same as changing it. Japanese schoolchildren still learn the Kyoho Reforms as the first of the three great reforms of the Edo period.

scenes.narration: Reporter's note. Today, Yoshimune lives on in popular culture. Long-running television dramas show a roaming, righteous shogun who disguises himself to put wrongs right, and the magistrate Ooka Tadasuke as a fair-minded judge. Those stories are fiction. What is documented is subtler: a ruler who inherited a financial crisis, made himself the first example, and then rebuilt the machinery of government around it. I think that is the paradox worth remembering. The most powerful man in Japan changed the country not through splendor, but by refusing it.

scenes.narration: Tokugawa Yoshimune never won a great battle, and he never led an army. He fought the quietest war a ruler can fight, against a deficit. He did not win it for good, but he gave his government a new lease on life. That kind of leadership rarely makes the headlines, yet it shapes nations.
